The Work, Torah Teaching and Linguistic Legacy of Menachem ben Saruq: A Philological, Hermeneutical and Historical Analysis of the Machberet Enterprise and the Andalusian Polemic
The work presents an in-depth analysis of the "Machberet Menachem," the first biblical Hebrew dictionary written in Hebrew, examining the work of Menachem ben Saruq against the background of Jewish patronage in Muslim Spain. The text details his distinctive linguistic theory, based on the principle of the stability and shedding of the root letters, and emphasizes his conservative hermeneutical approach, which sanctifies the Masoretic text and rejects comparisons with foreign languages. A central element of the account is the sharp Andalusian polemic with Dunash ben Labrat, which led to Menachem's personal downfall but gave rise to an extraordinary literary and emotional work in the form of his letter of protest. Finally, the article discusses the circulation of the work among the sages of Christian Europe, and especially its decisive influence on Rashi's commentary, which granted Menachem's teaching the status of an eternal linguistic authority in the Jewish bookshelf.
The Work, Torah Teaching and Linguistic Legacy of Menachem ben Saruq: A Philological, Hermeneutical and Historical Analysis of the Machberet Enterprise and the Andalusian Polemic
The Socio-Political Background of the Court of Cordoba and the Rise of Jewish Patronage
The study of the Hebrew language and biblical grammar in the tenth century in al-Andalus (Muslim Spain) was not an isolated academic enterprise, but a distinct expression of far-reaching geopolitical, cultural and theological transformations [cite: 1, 2]. With the rise of the Caliphate of Cordoba under the rule of Abd al-Rahman III, the gradual decline of the traditional Jewish center in Babylonia began, and at the same time an aspiration developed among the leadership of Spanish Jewry to establish an independent spiritual and Torah center, one that would free itself from economic and halakhic dependence on the Geonim of the East [cite: 2].
The central engine behind this trend was the Jewish statesman, physician and diplomat Hasdai ibn Shaprut, who served as the "nagid" of the Jewish community in the kingdom [cite: 2]. Hasdai, who operated from within the caliph's court, used his standing and his financial resources to invite to the court of Cordoba Torah scholars, poets and linguists from Babylonia and North Africa, and initiated the copying and dissemination of the Babylonian Talmud by means of scribes whom he hired [cite: 2]. This institution of patronage, which drew deep inspiration from the dominant Muslim culture, in which rulers and the wealthy customarily extended patronage to poets and scholars, gave scholars the quiet and the material means to devote themselves to developing the Science of Judaism [cite: 1].
Menachem ben Yaakov ibn Saruq was integrated into this social and scholarly network [cite: 1]. Menachem was born around the year 920 in the city of Tortosa in northeastern Spain, to a middle-class family engaged in commerce [cite: 1]. Menachem's family combined commercial activity with a traditional engagement in the science of language and the composition of piyyutim [cite: 1]. Menachem's reputation as a brilliant grammarian and liturgical poet reached the court of Cordoba, and he was invited to move there with his family under the patronage of Yitzchak ibn Shaprut, Hasdai's father [cite: 1]. Menachem served as Yitzchak's secretary and devoted himself to the study of Hebrew until the patron's death, whereupon he returned temporarily to Tortosa to engage in commerce [cite: 1, 3].
When Hasdai ibn Shaprut inherited his father's position and was appointed nagid, he summoned Menachem to return to Cordoba and promised him full support to complete his linguistic research [cite: 1, 3]. In his capacity as secretary of Hasdai's chancery, Menachem was in all likelihood the drafter of the renowned diplomatic and historical letter sent to Joseph, king of the Khazars, in which he managed to weave his own name into the acrostic of the opening poem, immediately after Hasdai's name [cite: 1, 4]. This relationship, based on complete dependence on the patron, formed the basis for Menachem's scholarly activity, but also paved the way for his tragic downfall in the wake of internal power struggles at the court [cite: 5, 6, 7].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Machberet Enterprise: The First Monolingual Hebrew Dictionary and the Ideology of Linguistic Independence
Between the years 950–960, Menachem completed his great linguistic work, the "Machberet Menachem" (from the word "chibbur," composition), which was in effect the first complete book of roots encompassing all the words of Scripture and of biblical Aramaic [cite: 1, 8]. To understand the magnitude of the revolution of the "Machberet," it must be compared with the lexicographical works that preceded it in Spain and in the East, which were written for the most part in Judeo-Arabic:
Table 1: A Structural and Methodological Comparison of the First Hebrew Dictionaries in the Middle Ages
From an analysis of the data in the table it emerges clearly that Menachem's choice to write the "Machberet" in Hebrew was an act of linguistic and cultural patriotism [cite: 8]. Menachem lived in an environment in which Arabic was the dominant language of science, government and philosophy, and he himself mastered it without limit [cite: 8]. Nevertheless, he refused to compare the words of Scripture with Arabic [cite: 8]. This decision stemmed from a theological conception that regards the Holy Tongue as a divine language standing on its own, chosen by God and not requiring the "assistance" of foreign tongues to clarify its meanings [cite: 1, 8]. Menachem held that Scripture explains itself best from its own internal contexts, and that the process of elucidation is carried out by adducing multiple examples of the same word in different contexts, while defining its varied linguistic senses [cite: 8, 10].
The only linguistic aid that Menachem permitted himself was the use of the Aramaic language [cite: 8]. In his view, Aramaic is not regarded as a wholly foreign language but as a related and sister tongue, which attained a certain holiness by virtue of its inclusion in the biblical text itself and in the literature of the Sages [cite: 8]. Accordingly, the "Machberet" makes use of biblical Aramaic, the Aramaic of the Targum Onkelos and the Aramaic of the Sages in order to explain difficult Hebrew words, and it interweaves the Aramaic entries among the Hebrew words without any structural partition [cite: 8].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Menachem's Theory of the Root: The Principle of Stability and Morphological Dynamics
The morphological method of Menachem ben Saruq rests on a physical phonetic-structural conception of the written word [cite: 8]. In contrast to the modern school, which assumes that every Hebrew root must be triconsonantal (a principle developed later by Yehuda Chayyuj) [cite: 8, 12, 13], Menachem held that the length of the root is dynamic and ranges from one letter to five letters [cite: 3, 8, 9].
The foundation of Menachem's method is the principle of stability and shedding [cite: 8]. Menachem determined that the true root letters are solely those letters that appear consistently and constantly in all the inflections, verbal patterns and forms of the word [cite: 8]. If a word inflects into a particular form in which one of the letters disappears, is omitted or is swallowed up, then that letter cannot be considered part of the root [cite: 8]. From this, several revolutionary rules were derived:
Identification of one-letter and two-letter roots: Menachem defined the root of the word nafal (נָפַל, "he fell") as only pe-lamed (פ"ל), since in the future form "yippol" (יִפּוֹל) the initial nun disappears [cite: 8]. In an even more extreme case, he identified the root of the words natah (נָטָה), matteh (מַטֶּה) and netiyyah (נְטִיָּה) as the letter tet (ט') alone, since in forms such as "yet" (יֵט) both the initial nun and the final he drop out, and only the tet remains as firm as a rock in all the occurrences [cite: 8].
Definition of the letters אהו"י (alef, he, vav, yod): Menachem established a rigid law for the letters vav and yod: they are recognized as root letters only if they are pronounced as hard consonants in all the occurrences of the entry [cite: 8]. As soon as in one of the occurrences the letter is pronounced as a mater lectionis (a vowel and not a consonant), it forfeits its status as a root letter [cite: 8]. Thus, in the word tavekh (תָּוֶךְ, "midst"), the vav is not a root letter, because in the word betokh (בְּתוֹךְ) it serves as a mater lectionis, and therefore the root of the word was determined to be tav-khaf (ת"ך) [cite: 8].
The role of the formative letters (servile letters): Menachem divides the formative letters (the letters of use) into two groups: the group תימנ"ה (tav, yod, mem, nun, he)—servile letters which, because of their position and function, may mislead and appear as though they were part of the root ("clinging with the grip of the essential") [cite: 11], and the group שלאכו"ב (shin, lamed, alef, kaf, vav, bet)—formative letters that never mislead and serve only as external formatives [cite: 11]. Menachem developed the rule of the "triple word," which holds that words with three stable root letters are strong and stand on their own strength, and have no need of servile letters, whereas the formative letters come to assist and support words with short roots (of one or two letters) in order to enable them to stand at the beginning or the end of the word [cite: 11].
The distinctiveness of the letter alef: Menachem identified the tendency of the alef to drop out of pronunciation and spelling in certain places [cite: 11]. In contrast to later grammarians, who saw in this proof of complex grammatical patterns, Menachem attributed it to the natural and light phonetic weakness of the letter, which physically omits itself from the word on account of its instability [cite: 11].
This conception led Menachem to frequently confuse verbs with nouns under the same lexical entry, since his classification was based not on semantic or syntactic categories but only on the phonetic-formal composition of the stable letters [cite: 11].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Hermeneutical Thought: The Sanctity of the Text, the Rejection of Alterations and the Attitude to the Sages
The Torah thought of Menachem ben Saruq was characterized by an attitude of reverence and extreme textual conservatism toward the biblical text [cite: 1, 8]. Menachem held an uncompromising hermeneutical conception that prevents any emendation, correction or alteration of the letters of Scripture for the purpose of resolving interpretive difficulties [cite: 8].
He came out sharply against exegetical schools (among them the approach of Rav Saadia Gaon and Yehuda ibn Quraysh) that made it easy for themselves in explaining difficult words by resorting to the interchange of letters or the transposition of letters [cite: 1, 8]. Menachem held that these methods harm the sanctity of the Masoretic text and could lead to the destruction of the language [cite: 1, 8].
The historian and linguist Yitzchak Isaac Halevi Weiss emphasized this hermeneutical pioneering, noting that Menachem foresaw almost "by divine inspiration" the rise of modern biblical criticism [cite: 1, 3]. Many modern solvers and critics, when they find unique words whose derivation they do not understand, tend to alter the letters, replace words and destroy the structure of the language—a phenomenon against which Menachem fought with all his might, out of an understanding that the integrity of the text takes precedence over interpretive convenience [cite: 3].
This conservative hermeneutics, which adheres consistently to the written form of Scripture (ketiv) and not to its reading tradition (qeri) [cite: 8], created an inherent tension between Menachem's interpretations and the halakhic interpretations of the Sages [cite: 8]. Menachem saw himself as committed to the pursuit of the philological truth of the plain meaning of Scripture, even when it did not accord with the halakhic derivation [cite: 3].
This gap found sharp expression in two central issues:
The interpretation of the word "totafot": The Sages interpreted this word as referring physically to the head tefillin on the basis of complex derivations. Menachem, by contrast, adhered to a purely philological analysis and derived the word from the root tet-pe (ט"ף), which denotes the uttering of law, memory and speech (from the expression "and preach toward the south") [cite: 8]. He explained the commandment as a spiritual-conceptual requirement to remember the laws of God, and not as a defined physical object [cite: 8].
The explanation of the term "u-malak": In the Book of Leviticus (1:15) it is said regarding the bird offering: "u-malak et rosho" (and he shall wring off its head). Whereas rabbinic halakha defines melikah as a distinctive cutting with the fingernail at the back of the neck, Menachem interpreted the word "u-malak" simply as an expression of ordinary slaughter, ignoring the complex halakhic distinction of the Sages [cite: 5, 6, 9].
Menachem's adherence to the dry linguistic plain meaning supplied his opponents with the strongest argument against him: the accusation of latent Karaite tendencies [cite: 1, 8]. At a time when the struggle against the Karaite movement was at its height, interpretations that deviated from rabbinic halakha and recalled Karaite methods of interpretation were perceived as an existential threat to the community [cite: 5, 6].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Scholarly and Personal Polemic: Dunash's Critiques and the Accusations of Heresy
Menachem's scholarly flourishing was cut short with the arrival in Cordoba of the grammarian and poet Dunash ben Labrat from Fez in Morocco [cite: 1, 3, 4, 5]. Dunash, who was educated in Babylonia under Rav Saadia Gaon, brought with him a radically different linguistic approach, deeply influenced by the methodology and the meters of Arabic poetry and grammar [cite: 5, 14]. Professional jealousy and deep scholarly disagreements prompted Dunash to compose his sharp book of critiques, "Dunash's Responses to Menachem," which contains some two hundred detailed critiques of the "Machberet" [cite: 5, 6, 8, 9].
Dunash chose to present his scholarly critiques in a dramatic fashion that would attract the attention of the patron, Hasdai ibn Shaprut [cite: 3, 5, 6]. He sent Hasdai the book accompanied by two principal poems:
"Ra'ah Libi": a poem of praise and glory for Hasdai, 41 verses long, intended to establish Dunash's standing as a new associate of the court [cite: 5].
"Ledoresh ha-Chokhmot": a scathing polemical poem, 110 verses long, directed squarely against Menachem [cite: 5]. In this poem Dunash poured scorn and disgrace on Menachem's head, called him a "simpleton," and accused him of gravely dishonoring his late teacher, Rav Saadia Gaon [cite: 5].
Beyond the linguistic disagreements (such as the division of specific roots and the use of patterns), Dunash used a political doomsday weapon: he accused Menachem of having an interpretation that encourages Karaite views and undermines accepted halakha [cite: 5, 6, 9]. Dunash pointed to Menachem's interpretation of the word "u-malak" as an expression of slaughter, and stressed to Hasdai that this interpretation is completely identical to that of Anan ben David, the founder of Karaism, thereby accusing Menachem of permitting the forbidden and forbidding the permitted [cite: 5, 6, 9].
This accusation, being hurled before Hasdai ibn Shaprut—who was zealous for preserving rabbinic orthodoxy in his kingdom—led to a complete reversal in his attitude toward Menachem [cite: 2, 5, 6]. Hasdai ceased his support of Menachem entirely, began to bear him deep enmity, and ordered his servants to expel him from his house with violence and humiliation in the midst of the Sabbath day [cite: 5, 6, 9].
The humiliated Menachem, who returned to Tortosa stripped of his possessions, sent Hasdai a heartrending letter of protest [cite: 3, 7]. Modern studies that analyzed the language of the letter (such as the study of Ariel Zinder, 2025) have revealed that it is a document of extraordinary literary and psychological value [cite: 7]. In the letter Menachem wove together intense expressions of emotion—rage, sorrow and hope—which constitute a complete innovation with regard to the writing accepted at that time [cite: 7]. He drew the legitimacy for this public emotional expression from two sources:
The Arabic patronage model: the tradition of Arabic "poems of complaint and apology," which define the emotional and moral relationship between the disappointed poet and his patron [cite: 7].
The biblical prayer model: an inner-Jewish discourse based on the unmediated relationship between the wronged person and his God, as reflected in the Book of Job and in Psalms, which combine direct address and a demand for justice [cite: 7].
This letter became a model of anthropocentric and theocentric writing that expresses the crisis of the individual in the face of tyrannical rule [cite: 7].
Table 2: The Central Interpretive and Halakhic Points of Dispute between Menachem and Dunash
It is interesting to note that despite the sharp dispute, Dunash himself underwent a process of moderation after the death of Hasdai ibn Shaprut [cite: 5]. In his later work "The Responses of Dunash ha-Levi ben Labrat to Rabbi Saadia Gaon," Dunash sharply criticized his former teacher for violating the rules of the Masorah [cite: 5]. Dunash made a declaration that brings him very close to Menachem's conservative position: "Heaven forbid that we should resolve anything that would lead us to violate a single point of the Holy Tongue" [cite: 5], a fact indicating that the original dispute ultimately contributed to raising the standing of Masoretic conservatism among all the schools [cite: 5].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Continuity of the Research: The War of the Disciples and the Transition to the Triconsonantal School
Menachem's physical downfall did not seal the fate of his school, but ignited a fierce generations-long struggle between his disciples and the disciples of Dunash [cite: 8, 9]. Menachem's distinguished disciples—Yitzchak ben Kafron, Yitzchak ibn Gikatilla and Yehuda ben David (who would later reveal himself as Yehuda Chayyuj)—united to defend the honor of their teacher and composed the monumental work "The Responses of the Disciples of Menachem" [cite: 1, 16]. They attacked Dunash chiefly for his use of the rules of Arabic grammar and poetry, which they regarded as a foreign intrusion that corrupts the eloquence of biblical Hebrew [cite: 5, 14]. On the other side, Yehudi ben Sheshet, a disciple of Dunash, came to the defense of his teacher and composed a sharp book of critiques saturated with personal rage ("The Responses of a Disciple of Dunash"), in which he tried to prove the scholarly superiority of Dunash's method [cite: 1, 14, 16].
However, the great historical irony of the Andalusian polemic lies in the figure of Rabbi Yehuda Chayyuj [cite: 8, 12, 13]. Chayyuj, who began his scholarly path as a disciple of Menachem defending his teacher against Dunash [cite: 1, 12], was the one who in the end brought about the collapse of Menachem's morphological school [cite: 8, 12, 13].
Chayyuj traveled to Cordoba in the midst of the debate, and understood that Menachem's old definition of the root (defined solely by the stable letters) prevents the development of a consistent and scientific grammatical system [cite: 12, 13]. He was exposed to the fact that the Arabic grammarians had already discovered in the eighth century the triliteral nature of roots [cite: 12], and understood that the Hebrew language operates according to similar laws [cite: 8, 12, 13]. Chayyuj brought about a dramatic breakthrough when he established that all Hebrew roots are triconsonantal (consisting of at least three letters) [cite: 8, 12, 13].
The physical disappearance of letters (such as the nun in "yippol" or the alef and the he in "yet") Chayyuj explained by means of fixed phonetic laws governing the behavior of the weak letters אהו"י (alef, he, vav, yod) ("the quiescent weak," ha-nach ha-rafeh) and the rules of the assimilation of the nun (verbs with an initial nun, chasrei pe-nun) [cite: 8, 12, 17]. He established and elaborated his revolutionary method in four foundational books that he wrote in Arabic:
Kitab al-Tanqit (the Book of Vocalization): deals with the laws of vocalization and the patterns of nouns (translated into Hebrew by Ibn Ezra) [cite: 12].
Kitab al-Af'al dhawat huruf al-Lin (the Book of Verbs with Weak Letters): deals with verbs of the weak root classes (pe-yod, ayin-vav, lamed-he) and explains their triliteral nature [cite: 12, 13].
Kitab al-Af'al dhawat al-Mithlayn (the Book of Verbs with Doubling): deals with the class of geminate roots (ayin-ayin) [cite: 12, 13].
Kitab al-Nutaf (the Book of Baldness): a sophisticated grammatical commentary on the difficult words in the books of the Prophets, applying the principle of triconsonantality [cite: 12, 13, 17].
In doing so, Chayyuj in practice followed the methodological path of Dunash (comparison with Arabic and the use of patterns) [cite: 12, 14], but preserved Menachem's reverence for the Masorah [cite: 8]. Chayyuj's great successor, Rabbi Yonah ibn Janach, refined this method and made it the foundation of Hebrew grammar accepted to this day [cite: 11, 12, 13].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Reception of the "Machberet" in Christian Europe: Rashi's Use and the Rulings of Rabbenu Tam
Although the triconsonantal school of Chayyuj and Ibn Janach rapidly conquered the scholarly centers in Muslim Spain and North Africa [cite: 2, 13], among the Jewish communities in the Christian lands (France, Ashkenaz and Italy) Menachem's "Machberet" attained an unprecedented status of exclusive linguistic authority [cite: 3, 10, 18].
The main reason for this was the language of the work [cite: 3, 10]. The sages of Christian Europe did not master the Arabic language, and therefore the works of Chayyuj and Ibn Janach, which were written in Judeo-Arabic, were closed to them [cite: 3]. Menachem's "Machberet," which was written in clear and eloquent biblical Hebrew, constituted for them the only systematic lexical and grammatical tool for understanding Scripture [cite: 3, 10].
Menachem's Influence on Rashi's Commentary on the Torah
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (Rashi), the greatest of the biblical commentators, regarded Menachem as the supreme authority in matters of grammar and language [cite: 3]. Rashi used the "Machberet" as a kind of daily working dictionary in composing his commentaries on Scripture and the Talmud, and he mentions Menachem by name in over 170 different places [cite: 8, 19].
Bibliographic and textual studies (such as those of Berliner and Filipowski) have revealed that Menachem's influence on Rashi is far deeper than appears on the surface [cite: 20]. Rashi incorporated into his commentaries Menachem's morphological method and definitions in dozens of places without explicitly mentioning his name ("silent citation") [cite: 20]. This fact becomes clear when Rashi's commentaries on the Torah are compared with his commentaries elsewhere (such as on Psalms or the Talmud), where he gives exactly the same explanation but attributes it explicitly to Menachem [cite: 20].
Clear examples of Rashi's silent citations from the "Machberet" include:
Exodus 28:28 ("ve-yirkesu et ha-choshen," and they shall bind the breastplate): Rashi connects this word with the words "mei-rukhsei ish" (Psalms 31:21) and interprets them as an expression of joining, exactly as Menachem connected them in the "Machberet," but without mentioning his name [cite: 20].
Lamentations 1:4 ("betulotehah nugot"): Rashi explains that there is in the word "nugot" no root of sorrow (yagon), but that the letter gimel alone is the root (according to Menachem's method of one-letter roots), without citing Menachem by name [cite: 20].
2 Samuel 19:10 ("va-yehi kol ha-am nadon"): Rashi interprets this word as an expression of "arguing with one another," according to Menachem's morphological definition, without indicating the source [cite: 20].
Ezra 4:12 ("ve-ushaiya yachitu"): Rashi interprets "yachitu" as an expression of thread and joining, like Menachem, without mentioning his name [cite: 20].
In this way Rashi became the chief disseminator of Menachem's teaching in northern Europe, and granted the "Machberet" eternal life in the study halls [cite: 8].
The Philological Defense of Rabbenu Tam
Rashi's grandson, Rabbi Yaakov ben Meir (Rabbenu Tam), decided to set out on a scholarly campaign to defend Menachem's honor against the critiques of Dunash [cite: 6, 8, 14]. Rabbenu Tam composed the "Sefer ha-Hachra'ot" (the Book of Rulings) [cite: 6, 14, 15]. In this sophisticated work Rabbenu Tam went over the disputes between the two giants of language, and in the overwhelming majority of cases sided with Menachem and answered Dunash's claims [cite: 6, 8, 14]. Rabbenu Tam sought to prove that Menachem's linguistic solutions do not contradict the halakhic tradition but constitute pure linguistic plain meaning, which separates verbal analysis from halakhic application [cite: 5, 6].
This polemic continued to occupy the sages of Europe in the following century as well: Rabbi Yosef Kimchi (the father of the Radak) composed the "Sefer ha-Galui" (the Book of the Revealed) in order to defend, specifically, Dunash's positions against the rulings of Rabbenu Tam [cite: 6, 14]. The Sefer ha-Galui is divided into two parts: the first part clarifies the differences between the two and includes responses to Rabbenu Tam's rulings (in which are interwoven glosses under the pseudonym "and I, Binyamin," defending Rabbenu Tam in return), and the second part includes independent glosses on Menachem's words in places where Dunash did not respond to them [cite: 6].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Manuscript Tradition and the Scholarly Editions
Evidence of the enormous popularity of the "Machberet" over the generations is the wealth of textual witnesses that have survived and reached us [cite: 8]. In contrast to many medieval scholarly works that were lost, the "Machberet Menachem" has a very extensive surviving textual tradition:
Complete manuscripts: some 20 complete manuscripts of the "Machberet" have reached us, located in libraries and research institutions around the world, from Moscow and Kraków in the east to London and Oxford in the west [cite: 8]. The oldest manuscript known to us is dated to the 11th century and is located in London [cite: 1].
The Cairo Genizah: some 22 leaves of fragments of the "Machberet" were discovered in the Cairo Genizah, attesting that the book was widespread and accepted in the regions of the Middle East and North Africa as well, despite the dominance of the triconsonantal school in those regions [cite: 8]. Most of these manuscripts are now held in microfilm format at the Institute of Microfilmed Hebrew Manuscripts of the National Library in Jerusalem [cite: 8].
In the early modern period and the modern era the "Machberet" appeared in three major scholarly editions, which indicate the development of philological research:
The edition of Zvi Filipowski (London and Edinburgh, 1854): published by the "Me'orerei Yeshenim" society (Awakeners of the Sleepers) [cite: 8]. This is the first printed edition of the "Machberet," which was prepared on the basis of the few manuscripts that were accessible at the time, and it was a breakthrough in making the work accessible to scholars of the Science of Judaism in the 19th century [cite: 8]. Important notes and additions by the scholar David Kaufmann were added to this edition [cite: 3].
The critical edition of Ángel Sáenz-Badillos (Granada, 1986): a modern and meticulous critical edition prepared by the Spanish linguist Sáenz-Badillos (Angel Sáenz-Badillos) [cite: 8]. This edition was based on a painstaking comparison of all the known manuscripts and the Genizah leaves, and it is regarded as a cornerstone of the modern study of Andalusian Hebrew linguistics [cite: 1, 8].
The edition of Aharon Maman and Chananel Mirsky (Jerusalem, 2024): the most scholarly and comprehensive edition published [cite: 8]. This edition includes, alongside the corrected text, a detailed and in-depth commentary, which presents synchronic and anachronistic comparisons between Menachem's linguistic interpretations and those of Rav Saadia Gaon, David ben Abraham Alfasi, Rabbi Yonah ibn Janach and Rashi [cite: 8]. This edition enables scholars to identify the lines of continuity and change in Jewish linguistic thought over the generations [cite: 8].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary and Conclusions
Menachem ben Saruq represents a figure of a hermeneutical and linguistic pioneer who operated at the seam between the Geonic period and the Golden Age of Spanish Jewry [cite: 1]. Although his morphological theory concerning the dynamic length of the root was ultimately displaced by the triconsonantal root theory of Chayyuj and Ibn Janach [cite: 8, 12, 13], his contribution to the study of the Hebrew language remained eternal [cite: 3, 8].
Menachem's groundbreaking decision to compose the "Machberet" in the Hebrew language alone set up an ideological and scholarly barrier against the influence of Arabic, and thereby opened a unique gateway for the sages of Christian Europe (headed by Rashi) to absorb the achievements of Andalusian linguistics [cite: 3, 10]. His uncompromising textual conservatism, his defense of the integrity of the Masorah against alterations and transpositions of letters, and his independent pursuit of the plain meaning of Scripture—even when it clashed with the homilies of the Sages—shaped the methodology of biblical study for generations [cite: 3, 8].
Menachem's personal tragedy, which was exploited by his rivals for false political accusations of heresy, gave rise to one of the most brilliant emotional and literary letters of the Middle Ages [cite: 5, 6, 7], and set up a model example of a scholar who holds fast to his scholarly and religious truth despite persecution by the authorities [cite: 7]. His linguistic legacy, which won the defense of Rabbenu Tam and meticulous preservation in Rashi's commentary [cite: 8, 20], forms an integral part of the Jewish bookshelf and of the process of the revival of the Hebrew language [cite: 8].
